stories.headline: WNBA Finals guide: Dream-Valkyries predictions and how each team could win
stories.summary: Expect a defensive master class as Gabby Williams and Golden State battle Angel Reese and Atlanta for the title.
stories.byline: Michael Voepel and Alexa Philippou and Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland
stories.body:
After joining the WNBA as an expansion team in 2008, it took the Atlanta Dream three seasons to make the WNBA Finals. The Golden State Valkyries, who debuted in 2025, reached the Finals in their second season.

One of them will become a first-time WNBA champion before the end of the month. The best-of-seven WNBA Finals open Saturday (3:30 p.m. ET) at Chase Center in San Francisco.

The No. 2 seed Valkyries -- who will host Games 1, 2 and, if necessary, 5 and 7 -- are coming off a semifinals sweep of the defending champion Las Vegas Aces, while the No. 4 Dream swept the New York Liberty. Both those series ended Oct. 9, giving Golden State and Atlanta plenty of prep time ahead of Game 1.

Expect defense to dominate the Finals, as the Valkyries and Dream were rated Nos. 1 and 2 in defense this season. While the Valkyries appear to be healthy, Dream guard Allisha Gray -- limited to 11 minutes in Game 1 of the semifinals because of an injury on her shooting hand (left) -- has said she is day-to-day after undergoing a recent procedure.

The Dream enter the Finals on a 10-game winning streak. Golden State won the regular-season series 3-0, but their last meeting was July 4.

Atlanta is making its fourth WNBA Finals appearance, but was swept in 2010, 2011 and 2013. Now the Dream will attempt to turn that disappointing history into an October celebration. And the Valkyries will try to join their NBA brethren Golden State Warriors as a league champion.

ESPN breaks down how the teams match up and predicts which team will hoist the trophy.

Jump to: GS | ATL | Key questions | Picks

(2) Golden State Valkyries

How Golden State got here

The Valkyries are the first team in league history to make the WNBA Finals within the first two years of its franchise launch. They beat the Dallas Wings in three games in the best-of-three first-round series and then swept Las Vegas in the semifinals. Golden State is 5-1 this postseason, with the lone loss being Game 2 on the road against the Wings, when Wings guard Arike Ogunbowale had 45 points.

The Valkyries have looked unflappable since then. In the first game of the semifinals, they held the Aces to a season-low 60 points and were plus-27 on the boards (grabbing a franchise-record 52 rebounds, including 17 offensive). In Game 3, the Valkyries rallied from their first double-digit deficit of the series to win in overtime. Gabby Williams has continued her breakout season and is the leading scorer remaining this postseason, averaging 22.7 points. Kiah Stokes is the series' leading rebounder with 9.5 per game. -- Kendra Andrews

Golden State's projected starters

G Veronica Burton (9.5 PPG)

F Kayla Thornton (10.8 PPG)

F Gabby Williams (22.7 PPG)

F Cecilia Zandalasini (8.5 PP)

C Kiah Stokes (9.5 RPG)

What we're hearing about the Valkyries

After becoming the first expansion team to make the playoffs in its inaugural season, the Valkyries were primed for greater success in Year 2 -- and aren't surprised to be here. "This is unimaginable, but for us it's so realistic," Burton said after the Valkyries swept the Aces. "It's what we expected and what we've worked for. It's what we believed in the entire year."

The players developed an immediate bond and chemistry. Part of that they credit to a clear game plan and vision from the top of the organization down, but also to the roster being made up of many players unwanted by their previous clubs.

"A lot of us bounced around, and that's what makes it special," Thornton said. "A lot of us have been denied. ... When you bring this group together, we create something big. We do it for each other because we know what we've been through."

But as a group, the Valkyries don't have championship experience. Only four players on the roster have competed for a WNBA title: Thornton (2024), Tiffany Hayes (2023), Zandalasini (2024) and Stokes (2022, 2023, 2025). Coach Natalie Nakase was an assistant on Las Vegas' first two title teams.

"We have other WNBA champs, we have other Olympians," Williams said. "We all know how to get it done, we just now have to get it done together." -- Andrews

Why the Valkyries can win the title

Golden State's depth will be its superpower in this series. After having the best second unit in the WNBA throughout the regular season, the Valkyries' bench is scoring a league-best 32.3 points in the playoffs. The Dream's starting lineup has been the best scoring group in the postseason, but their bench averages 16.2 points. One of the biggest luxuries the Valkyries have is never knowing exactly who will go off from game to game -- but always knowing someone will.

Janelle Salaun won Sixth Player of the Year but has experienced a quiet postseason. Instead, Hayes has provided a massive spark off of the bench (13.3 PPG in the playoffs vs. 9.0 in the regular season), while Kaitlyn Chen and Kaila Charles have had momentum-swinging spurts. In Game 3 of the first round, Burton was benched after air-balling consecutive shots, but the Valkyries didn't miss a beat, a luxury many teams don't have.

If the Dream are without Gray, it shrinks Atlanta's depth and gives the Valkyries' already dominant depth more of an advantage. -- Andrews

If they win, the Finals MVP will be...

This might be the easiest question in this preview. The addition of Williams took the Valkyries from a playoff team to a championship contender. She finished No. 2 in Defensive Player of the Year voting and made a defense that was already elite in 2025 (ranked No. 3 with a 99.8 defensive rating) even better (No. 1 with a 99.1 rating, with no other club being better than 103.0). During the first two rounds, she averaged 22.7 points (No. 5 of all players in the postseason), 4.8 rebounds, 4.0 assists (No. 9) and 1.7 steals (No. 6). All of those metrics have increased from the regular season, including more than 8.0 points per game. She's shooting 40.5% from behind the arc and her 2.8 3-pointers per game ranks No. 4 in the playoffs and is the highest among those still playing.

Williams is one of the most well-rounded players in the league, and her addition gave the Valkyries a starter who could consistently create her own shot in one-on-one situations, something that was missing with Golden State. She has been the biggest difference in this 2026 Valkyries squad to the point that owner Joe Lacob, after an incredible Game 1 of the semifinals, declared Williams the best player in the world. -- Kareem Copeland

If they lose, it will be because ...

The Dream find cracks in the Valkyries' defense. Golden State has allowed more than 81 points just once in the playoffs. In the five victories, opponents averaged 74.2 points. The Valkyries aren't just an offensive juggernaut but are four wins from holding the trophy due to a stifling defense that feeds the offense. If Dream coach Karl Smesko can figure out a way to get clean looks for Rhyne Howard, Gray (if available), Jordin Canada and DeWanna Bonner, and if Angel Reese can be successful against Stokes, that's a significant advantage. Golden State isn't exactly built for shootouts, and Atlanta has averaged 92.6 points this postseason. -- Copeland

Player ready for Finals spotlight

Stokes is familiar with the Finals, less so with the spotlight. But she deserves her time to shine. Stokes started just seven games at UConn but won three NCAA titles. The No. 11 draft pick in 2015 by New York, she stayed with the Liberty until being waived in June 2021. Two days later, Las Vegas signed her. She won three WNBA championships with the Aces. Now she's a key part of the Valkyries, starting all season for them.

Stokes' commitment to doing whatever a team needs has made her a valuable veteran, and it can be easy for her to get lost in the shuffle because she doesn't score a lot (3.6 PPG in the regular season, 3.2 in playoffs). But the screens she sets, the passes she makes, plus the defense and rebounding are so big toward Golden State's success. She's coming off one of her best games of the season, with 11 points, 10 rebounds, three blocks, three assists and two steals in Golden State's 87-77 Game 3 win over the Aces. -- Michael Voepel

(4) Atlanta Dream

How Atlanta got here

The Dream have been the most dominant team in the postseason, winning five consecutive games and sweeping the Washington Mystics and New York. They defeated the Mystics by an average of 16.5 points before things became a bit more challenging against the 2024 WNBA champs. Despite losing leading scorer Gray (19.0 PPG in regular season) in Game 1 of the semis, Atlanta still won by 10. Overtime was required in Game 2, and the Dream won Games 2 and 3 by a combined five points.

Angel Reese is playing the best basketball of her career after being named Defensive Player of the Year. She is averaging 18.0 points, 8.4 rebounds, 2.2 blocks, 2.0 assists and 1.6 steals in the playoffs. Bonner has stepped into the starting lineup without Gray, whose status remains unknown for the Finals. Bonner, a veteran with 103 games of playoff experience, has been a perfect late-season addition. (Atlanta signed her in late August.) Canada has continued to be a defensive pest with 2.2 steals per game, which ties Howard for a 2026 postseason high, and she has increased her scoring average from 11.6 points in the regular season to 19.2 in the playoffs. -- Copeland

Atlanta's projected starters

G Jordin Canada (19.2 PPG)

G Rhyne Howard (19.2 PPG)

F Angel Reese (18.0 PPG)

F Naz Hillmon (5.2 PPG)

F DeWanna Bonner (13.2 PPG)

What we're hearing about the Dream

The Dream's 10 consecutive victories match the 2017 Sparks for the league's longest win streak entering the WNBA Finals. They are also a league-best 22-4 since a 10-point loss at home to the Portland Fire on July 11, which was their sixth loss in seven games.

The Dream credit a confluence of factors for allowing them to play their best basketball when it matters most. "I thought we had a really good [FIBA] break where we got to focus on some things," Smesko said Friday. "We had some players that got to play in the World Cup, and they all did really well. So I think they came back with a lot of confidence, and obviously adding [Bonner] added another dimension to our team.

"I just think we've been improving steadily through the season, and everybody's had a good attitude about getting better, and we've been able to play really well for a nice stretch here."

Reese and Canada have played some of the best basketball in their careers recently, but the group also attributes its hot streak to strong chemistry, something that has stood out to Bonner. "We are a really close group," she said. "I feel like I've been here since the beginning. I don't think there's a day that we don't want to come in here and come to work with each other and step on this court for each other."

With two titles apiece, Bonner and Canada are the only regular contributors who have won WNBA championships, Bonner with the Phoenix Mercury and Canada with the Seattle Storm. For Canada, those Storm championship teams boasted an off-court chemistry that translated onto the court.

"We've hung out, had team dinners, doing anything that we can to build bonds. And I think that means a lot more when you get to know a group on a deeper level outside of basketball and knowing who they are as people and what makes them go," Canada said. "Then in moments like this, when you're in such a heated moment or a heated series, you want to fight and you want to battle for the girl on the left and right of you." -- Alexa Philippou

Why the Dream can win the title

Even without Gray, Atlanta is the more offensively blessed team in this Finals matchup. Howard (17.7 PPG in the regular season) and Gray (19.0 PPG) are the two best offensive threats in this series and can win games on their own. Both ranked in the top 11 in scoring this season. Reese has continued to develop her offensive game, and the Dream have no problem running things through her, whether she's initiating it on the perimeter or catching it in the post. Canada's increased production adds another wrinkle into the Dream scheme while making up for the loss of Gray. Bonner, 39, is simply one of the best scorers in the history of the league, and she still has bursts that can bury an opponent.

Atlanta also loves to get out in transition off its aggressive defense that led the league in steals (9.1 per game). In the semifinals, the Dream scored 60 points off 38 turnovers in the first two games. The biggest question, which the Valkyries have answered in each round, is if the league's top defense can continue to contain some of the best offenses? -- Copeland

If they win, the Finals MVP will be...

Reese or Canada. Reese has been the motor of this squad throughout the season. She outdueled Jonquel Jones in the Liberty series, averaging 20.7 points, 7.7 rebounds, 2.3 blocks and 2.0 steals. She plays with a tenacity and toughness that reverberate through the rest of the Dream. Per Elias, her 18.0 PPG in the postseason are on pace to be the fifth-highest average in WNBA history for a player making the Finals in their first playoff run.

Canada has been referred to as the head of the snake in Atlanta and has been its X factor this postseason: Her 19.2 points per game in the playoffs are well above her regular-season average (11.6 points) and are tied with Howard for best on the team. She's achieving that with stellar efficiency -- 51.6% from the field (33-of-64), 50% from 3-point range (12-of-24) and at the free throw line (18-of-18) -- all while quarterbacking the offense (8.8 assists) and defense (2.2 steals per game). -- Phillipou

If they lose, it will be because ...

Atlanta can't generate offense off Golden State turnovers and gets hurt by its lack of depth. The Dream's defensive pressure makes them elite at forcing turnovers and turning them into points: They were No. 1 in the league in steals per game (9.1) and points off turnovers in the regular season (18.1), and No. 2 in fast-break points (11.9). But Golden State excels in taking care of the ball: During the regular season, the Valkyries' 11.5 turnovers per game were fewest in the league, and in the playoffs that number is even lower (10.3, second to Dream's 9.0).

The Dream not nearly as deep as the Valkyries. Golden State's bench averaged 35.9 points in the regular season versus Atlanta's 17.9 PPG, one of the lowest marks in the league -- and that will be exacerbated even more if Gray cannot play. Golden State's litany of options could prove to be too much for an Atlanta squad that relies significantly on its starting five and could be without its top scorer. -- Phillipou

Player ready for Finals spotlight

Bonner left the Mercury to try to win a championship in what could be the final season of her career, and she's now four wins away. Most of the Dream players are relatively inexperienced on this stage. But Bonner -- who holds the league record for playoff games -- is not, and her leadership will be crucial for Atlanta to navigate the ups and downs of a seven-game series. Her offensive firepower (13.2 PPG in the playoffs) will be even more necessary for Atlanta if Gray can't play. -- Phillipou

Four key questions

How do the teams match up?

Atlanta has been great at forcing turnovers (17.2 per game) in its first two playoff series and converting those into points. That will be harder against Golden State, which has averaged just 9.2 turnovers in the playoffs. The Valkyries and the Dream (8.4) are the only two teams to average fewer than 10 turnovers in this postseason. Like so many things in this series, this is a strength vs. strength matchup.

That leads us to how the teams guard each other. Reese was the Defensive Player of the Year but A'ja Wilson is one of the best defensive players in WNBA history, and the Valkyries still figured out ways to get shots they wanted against her and the Aces in the semifinals -- and then convert enough of them.

The Valkyries' first two playoff opponents have been good preparation for facing the Dream in terms of how much Dallas and Las Vegas were able to challenge Golden State's defense. The Valkyries rose to that challenge. But neither the Wings nor the Aces presented as good of a defense as Atlanta brings.

So that should end up being the biggest key: Will the Valkyries find enough offensive success to win the championship? -- Voepel

What is the series X factor?

It could be health. Gray is one of the best players in the league. Even though the Dream won the semifinals with her playing only briefly before her Game 1 injury, she is a big absence. The Valkyries would have a different challenge guarding the Dream with Gray on the floor. Adding to her offensive repertoire, she's a very good defender and one of the most experienced players on the court. Gray is used to stepping up in big moments. If there is any way she can return to the Dream with some effectiveness, it could make a difference in this series. If not, the Valkyries' depth edge remains a key factor. -- Voepel

Ballhalla will boast 18,000-plus fans. The Dream aren't playing at their usual home arena. How much will home-court advantage be a factor?

As someone who has spent the better part of the past six months watching games in Ballhalla, there are very few home-court advantages such as what the Valkyries have at Chase Center. It isn't just that they have a raucous crowd or they've sold out every home game the past two seasons. The energy -- the rowdiness, the joy, the party -- makes it feel almost like a basketball utopia. Golden State went a league-best 17-5 at home during the regular season and it has yet to lose a game in San Francisco during these playoffs. The noise inside Chase Center is deafening, and it'll only get louder in the Finals. The Bay Area is built for playoff -- and championship -- basketball.

This isn't to say that Atlanta's home court won't be rocking. Adjusting the schedule to allow the Dream to play at State Farm Arena (which seats up to 17,000) rather than the 3,500-seat Gateway Arena was critical for the team and the league. While this isn't the Dream's usual home court, it's not unfamiliar. They played six regular-season games at State Farm and played all three postseason home contests there. There's a reason this was the only alternate venue the Dream wanted to play Finals games in. But for the Dream to win the Finals, they have to win at least one game on the road. That has been difficult in Ballhalla. -- Andrews

Will Atlanta's 0-3 record against Golden State in the regular season matter? What did we learn from those meetings?

Teams sometimes downplay prior results for a presumed strategic or motivational advantage. In this case, those games were so long ago, they don't have much bearing on what we're about to see.

All three meetings happened during an 11-day span from June 24 to July 4, with the first two games at Golden State and the third at Atlanta. It was during the worst stretch of the summer for the Dream, as they lost a season-high five games in a row.

In the first meeting, Atlanta was held to a season-low 66 points and shot 39% from the field, with Golden State making 15 3-pointers to the Dream's four. Back at Chase Center two days later, the Dream struggled even more from the field (34%). Atlanta got closer, but Golden State made enough free throws in the final minute to prevail.

After road losses at Seattle and Washington, the Dream took on Golden State again, this time in Atlanta. Once more, the Dream didn't shoot well (39%), although Gray, Howard and Reese combined for 58 points.

Atlanta didn't have Bonner for any of these games, and as a late addition, she has been a big difference-maker. Neither team is going to look back too much on what happened between them in the regular season as indicative of what's going to take place next. -- Voepel

WNBA Finals picks

Kendra Andrews: Golden State in 7. It's odd that the No. 2 team in the standings still feels like the underdog, but the Valkyries have proved time and again to never count them out. With a matchup of the top two defensive teams in the league, this series will be a slugfest, and the championship might come down to who can hit the last shot (or make the last stop). Not enough credit has been given to what the Valkyries have done on both sides of the ball this postseason. Watching what they did to the Aces showed they have another gear they can get to, and that will be crucial in this series.

Kareem Copeland: Atlanta in 7. The Dream have been held to fewer than 85 points just once since Aug. 28. Especially if Gray is back, the Valkyries will be challenged to shut down that offense four times in seven games. The Aces were short-handed and were more of a half-court-centered team on offense. Golden State wants to run off defensive stops, but Atlanta also wants to run as often as possible, even when taking the ball out of the net. A fast, up-tempo game would seem to favor the Dream.

Alexa Philippou: Golden State in 6. After seeing Atlanta dismantle the Liberty up close, the Dream were my pick to win it all as the team that has played the best basketball in the league by the end of the season. But my predictions have not aged well as we've progressed in the playoffs, so I'll go with the Valkyries continuing to make history and benefitting from their enormous home-court advantage at Ballhalla, including in a potential Game 7.

Michael Voepel: Golden State in 7. This isn't a fluke Finals matchup. The Valkyries were the No. 1 team in our final ESPN Power Rankings, and the Dream were fourth. Now they really do look like the best two teams after five months of physically and mentally grueling play. Both have played championship-worthy basketball in the postseason. Both coaches have been impressive in their preparation and adjustments. This pick is for two things that go Golden State's way: depth and home-court advantage for the series.

stories.headline: UCL Matchday 2: Viking FK and PSG impress; Man United a mess
stories.summary: The Chaaaaaampions! Europe's top competition returned with a ton of goals, a ton of big results and plenty to talk about. Let's start with the tiny Norwegian team that gave Bayern Munich a fright.
stories.body:
It is the way of the soccer world right now that competitions must get larger, with more teams, more matches per team and a much lower average reading on the jeopardy per match scale.

Aside from the obvious wear-and-tear concerns, I don't really mind this development. (Maybe it's the American in me: I'm used to bloat.)

I don't mind that the Euros have 24 teams, or that the Champions League has 36, or that the World Cup has 48 -- and that two-thirds of the competitors reach the knockout rounds in all of these tournaments. That has allowed for super-cool stories to develop.

Ukraine snuck into the knockout rounds at Euro 2020 (amid growing geopolitical stress) and then upset Sweden. Slovenia and Slovakia eked out advancement in 2024, too, and nearly pulled upsets. And while a huge Champions League with a huge set of knockout rounds has allowed more time for struggling powers like PSG and Manchester City in 2024-25 to rebound from poor starts, it also allowed Bodø/Glimt to find their footing and eventually take down Manchester City, Atlético Madrid and Inter Milan, consecutively, while nearly making the quarterfinals last season.

I don't mind bloat as long as it allows for proper storytelling and extra world-building. In a world with tilted finances, where only a few teams are actually capable of winning the whole thing, a fun journey almost matters more than the eventual destination.

Matchday 1 of this year's Champions League concerned me a bit in that regard. There was still fun to be had -- Como ran away from RB Leipzig in their first ever European group stage game, Real Madrid outlasted Inter Milan in a battle of European royalty, and 11 of 18 matches featured at least four goals. Goals are fun.

- UCL Talking Points: Who's to blame for Man United mess?

- Reaction: Man City can't compete with gold standard PSG

- Kirkland: Real Madrid did win, but glory feels far away

Still, Davids weren't exactly scoring damage points on Goliaths. PSG, Barcelona and Bayern Munich beat Slovan Bratislava, Feyenoord and Bodø/Glimt by a combined 16-2, and debutants LASK, Sabah and Viking all lost by a combined 8-1. It was a foreboding start, a sign that maybe Europe's giants have even further distanced themselves from the pack. I'm a fan of storytelling, and that's the least fun story to tell.

Luckily, Matchday 2 gave us delightful plot twists and track meets.

It also took us to Norway.

Main characters of the week

No. 1: Viking FK

Viking FK has lived a full club life since its founding in Stavanger in 1899: Early regional titles in the 1920s and 1930s; national titles in the 1950s, when that became a thing to aspire to; great spells (four straight titles in the 1970s); poor spells (relegation in 1986 and 2017); the requisite financial overextension in the 2010s (who among us).

On occasion, they've also enjoyed the glory of home European nights. They hosted Borussia Mönchengladbach (and drew 1-1) in the 1979-80 UEFA Cup, held Barcelona to a 0-0 draw in qualification for the inaugural 1992-93 Champions League) and walloped Sporting CP and drew with Werder Bremen in the 1999-2000 UEFA Cup. And in maybe the most famous night of the old Stavanger Stadion, they thumped Chelsea 4-2 in the 2002-03 UEFA Cup despite goals from Frank Lampard and John Terry.

Their current home, Viking Stadion, saw a win over Monaco in the 2005-06 UEFA Cup, plus a couple of fun victories in the 2022-23 Conference League. But after Tuesday, it's also the place where Viking hung three goals on -- and frustrated the hell out of -- Bayern Munich.

You have to take your victories where you can find them early in an eight-game Champions League league phase campaign, where the results aren't incredibly consequential and the surprises are minimal. But Viking vs. Bayern was an absolute blast. Viking ran the "score on your first shot" play -- every team should try that, it works out great for you -- and then went up 2-0 late in the first half. Bayern charged back because Bayern always charge back, but after a gorgeous Konrad Laimer-to-Luis Díaz goal gave the German giants the lead, Michael Olise got a red card, and it pretty visibly flipped the momentum in the match.

Herman Haugen headed in a tying goal over an unsuspecting Alphonso Davies (who probably should have been more suspecting), and Peter Christiansen forced a Jonas Urbig save in extra time. The stats for the game as a whole were one-sided (xG: Bayern 3.3, Viking 0.7), but when the match ended Viking appeared most likely to score next.

The Norwegian style of play might be the most aesthetically pleasing in the world at the moment: a mix of optimism and organization in attack, and a willingness to leave yourself a little exposed in the back. Bodø/Glimt have mastered this style and translated it well to European competitions -- they beat Borussia Dortmund on Wednesday to make it six straight home wins in the Champions League or Champions League qualification -- and Viking's first two Champions League league phase matches have featured 10 combined goals and a draw their fans will be talking about for ages.

I am a total sucker for stories like this.

And while we're celebrating teams that do everything possible to increase the pure entertainment value of the early stages, let's shout out Club Brugge, the watchability kings. So far they've lost 3-2 to Aston Villa and beaten Inter 4-3, and really, Tuesday's win undersold the amount of quality opportunities created: both teams underachieved against xG.

In 18 league phase matches since the start of 2024-25, they've scored multiple goals seven times and allowed multiple goals 10 times. They've won a match while allowing three, and they've drawn a match while scoring three. They are speed horses for this competition, and they are appreciated.

No. 2: Paris Saint-Germain

We're used to PSG taking their time shifting into gear in a given season. Luis Enrique has loads of both stars and incredible teenagers to give minutes to, and he knows he doesn't really have to find or lean on his best 11 until the spring. A few early losses won't exactly hurt them in Ligue 1, and two years ago they won the Champions League despite at one point going winless for four straight league phase matches.

They started this season in a little too much of a funk, however, with a loss to Lens in the Trophée des Champions and just two points in their first three Ligue 1 matches. They were tied for 13th with Le Mans after three league matchdays. That's a bit much.

Luckily, they know how to shift into gear.

In their past five matches on each side of the international break, they've won five matches by a combined 16-5. Enrique's still rotating like crazy -- 20 different guys have started in these five matches -- but PSG's ridiculous depth almost requires him to, and everyone's contributing. Ousmane Dembélé has three goals and four assists in four starts in this span, Ferran Torres has five goals, newcomer Maghnes Akliouche has two goals and an assist, Désiré Doué (who's still only 21, by the way) has a goal and two assists. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia hasn't contributed much, but PSG has still turned into a wrecking ball.

They seemed to have a point to prove Wednesday in Manchester.

Visiting fellow petrol staters Manchester City, who are staring potentially epic penalties in the face, PSG went up 2-0 within 15 minutes thanks to goals from Doué and Dembélé and got a third from midfielder Vitinha before halftime. After Erling Haaland pulled one back for the home team, Akliouche put away an eventual 4-2 win with a goal in the 62nd minute.

City had won eight straight matches in all competitions and had humiliated Liverpool 3-0 at Anfield over the weekend, but PSG basically scored an early-round knockout. The xG figures favored City (2.6 to 1.8), but that can be pretty common when one team takes an early lead. At the time of Vitinha's goal, PSG had attempted eight of the match's 10 shots with a higher volume of touches in the attacking third. They were incredible, and they didn't need long to put the match away.

No. 3: Manchester United

In a way, Manchester United's 2-0 away loss to Atlético Madrid was like just about any other United match in 2026-27, in that the underlying stats that are usually pretty predictive weren't at all. Their xG differential was +0.8 in their 2-0 loss to Hull City to kick off the Premier League season, and in three matches with near-even xGDs, they've lost once with two draws. They're sixth in the Premier League in xG differential but 13th in the table, and at the time of Leny Yoro's 74th-minute red card in Madrid, they trailed 1-0 with a plus-0.4 xGD. (Atleti also ran the "Score on your first shot" play. I'm just saying, it's a great play!) The match turned one-sided after that.

Poor fortune and random, debilitating mistakes are wrecking United's season when they really don't look too poor on paper.

Of course, United's players evidently have their own theory of what's going wrong, one revealed by Lisandro Martínez in postgame interviews. "We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete, because many teams bring many players as well," he said. "Atlético have an amazing team and they deserved to win today, but I expect more [investment] -- 100%. I expect more from our technical director."

Now, I know that other clubs have invested more than Manchester United in recent years, legally and illegally, and Martinez also made an interesting point about not "[staying] with what you did last season" because opponents always adjust. But despite the Premier League generally losing its mind from the perspective of cumulative transfer fees, I'm never going to see "completely rebuilding your midfield for €173.2 million," as United did this past summer, as a lack of investment or a simple "run it back" approach. United brought in Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans in to address last year's biggest question mark; that's a pretty big change! And they've spent €1.1 billion in transfer fees alone over the past five years. A competent organization should be able to build a perfectly stable team with that.

Even if it's not really a lack of investment, though, United have definitely suffered from a lack of a plan, and it's made competent investment nearly impossible. There's been no ideological consistency in their managerial hires, and their common lineup this season includes two guys who signed or debuted for Louis van Gaal, one for Jose Mourinho, two for Ole Gunnar Solskjær, two for Erik ten Hag, three for Ruben Amorim and one for Michael Carrick. That's a diverse set of influences, and it can't be a surprise when a lack of a plan produces a lack of cohesiveness. But I guess none of what I'm saying is all that original, is it?

No. 4: Serie A

There are nine leagues with multiple Champions League entries this season. Three of them are averaging at least 2.0 points per game among their teams in the field: England's Premier League (2.4), Spain's LaLiga (2.4) and Germany's Bundesliga (2.0). After a perfect 5-for-5 in the wins department in Matchday 1 (followed by a 3-for-3 performance in the Europa League), the Premier League gave away some points this week thanks to the clubs in Manchester.

Four more leagues are averaging at least 1.0 points per game among their teams: France's Ligue 1 (1.5), Portugal's Primeira Liga (1.5), the Netherlands' Eredivisie (1.0) and Norway's Eliteserien (1.0). Hell yeah, Norway. Hanging out with the big boys.

Granted, some of those league successes are coming from one team -- PSG has six of Ligue 1's nine points, and Sporting CP has all six of the Primeira Liga's -- but it's still pretty damn noteworthy that we've gotten this far down the list without mentioning Serie A. After this week's oh-fer, with four losses from four matches, Italian teams now have four points from their first eight matches. Como thumped RB Leipzig in their Champions League home debut in September, and Roma managed a draw against a Fenerbahce team that got blown out by Aston Villa on Wednesday, and that's it.

Now, it's probably not as awful as it seems. Roma played well for 80 minutes against Real Madrid before getting Real Madrid'd at the end for a 4-3 defeat, and Como (lost 3-2 to Feyenoord), Inter (4-3 to Brugge) and Napoli (3-1 to Villarreal) all had at least slightly positive xG differentials, meaning that while their finishing lacked, they were creating equal or better chances than their opponents. But this is still a dire start for a league that has produced just one quarterfinalist in the last three tournaments. (Granted, Inter made the finals in 2025. But that's still it.)

Through two matches each, all four Italian teams have allowed at least two goals from high turnovers, and Roma are one of two teams (along with LASK) to have allowed three. Combined with the fact that the teams are a combined minus-2 in set piece goal differential, you could start to put together a case that Serie A teams aren't really keeping up with the tactical times. But I'll let that one marinate a bit longer before pursuing it further.

Best players of Matchday 2

One thing I like to do if I miss a given match is look at each player's combined xG + xPVA to see who did the most dangerous things in that match. I assume you know xG by now, but xPVA is basically everything else a player did to increase their team's chances of winning (or Expected Point Value), beyond shot attempts - passes, ball recoveries, tackles, et cetera. It's a useful at-a-glance tool, and I figured I'd share the top 15 most dangerous players of Matchday 2.

I enjoy that this is such a mix of expected and unexpected players. It's definitely not a surprise to see Liverpool's Bradley Barcola and Brugge's Nicolo Tresoldi making the list after their respective hat tricks, though Tresoldi evidently produced negative xPVA -- no progressive passes or carries or really anything else, just shots that went into the net. (And hey, if you're only going to do one thing, that's a good one.)

It probably also isn't a surprise that there are two other Brugge players on the list (Carlos Forbs and Romeo Vermant) considering how well they tore apart Inter's midfield. Lautaro had a brace against Brugge, but he could have had so much more: He attempted 12 shots worth 3.0 xG and put nine of those shots on goal. It was honestly one of the most prodigious performances you'll ever see.

There are plenty of familiar names elsewhere -- Erling Haaland, Atleti's Ademola Lookman, Arsenal's Eberechi Eze, Bayern's Luis Diaz -- but among the others let's shout out LASK's Florian Flecker (two goals in 45 minutes against Liverpool), Slavia's Lukás Provod (eight shots worth 1.4 xG, four on target, but somehow no goals) and Fenerbahce's Vedat Muriqi (two shots worth 0.9 xG).

And now, the Power Rankings

This is purely who I would pick if teams were playing this weekend.

1. Barcelona. Two wins and a 9-2 scoring margin thus far. In fact, in all competitions this season they have a perfect 10 wins from 10 matches, with a 43-9 scoring margin. Forty-three! Raphinha has 14 goals and three assists! Lamine Yamal has eight and nine! Fermín López has five and two! Karim Adeyemi has four and two! Anthony Gordon has two and four! Barca are pressing, passing and shooting better than ever, and while we'll have to wait and see if Hansi Flick's high-wire style can win a long series of knockout rounds, there is no question who the best team in Europe is at the moment.

We'll see if we're still saying that after next week: They visit PSG on Tuesday, then host Real Madrid for the first El Clásico of the season on Sunday.

2. PSG. Still only up to sixth in Ligue 1. I doubt they're worried.

3. Arsenal. Methodical and confident.

4. Bayern Munich. I'm not worried about them, but I'm not sure the "allow a goal in the first two minutes every match" approach of the last week is a good thing. (Missing Olise to a red card suspension for next week's Arsenal match stinks.)

5. Manchester City. Crush Liverpool and then get crushed by PSG. A pretty extreme week after a pretty extreme few weeks.

6. Real Madrid. If this isn't a damn "Real Madrid in the Champions League" chart, I don't know what is.

7. Aston Villa. After only one win in their first six matches in all competitions, they're now unbeaten in five, and they've scored 17 goals in the process.

8. Liverpool. It took Bradley Barcola until his seventh match to score in Liverpool red, but a hat trick made up for lost time.

9. Sporting CP. They haven't lost since April, and they've won each of their first two Champions League matches by multiple goals.

10. Atlético Madrid. Five straight wins since the loss to Liverpool.

11. VfB Stuttgart. They were handed a pretty light start -- Viking, at Slovan Bratislava -- and made the most of it with two easy wins. The challenges start with a visit from Atlético next week, but they're already two-thirds of the way toward advancing to the knockouts.

12. Real Betis. Two matches, two 3-2 wins. They drew 67,114 to the Estadio La Cartuja for the win over Porto on Wednesday, and it sounded like 100,000.

13. Borussia Dortmund. After six straight wins before the international break, they have a draw and a loss since. Someone always gets hit by the post-break funk.

14. Manchester United. I'm ranking them 14th because they're basically eighth and 20th at the same time.

15. Club Brugge. Averaging three goals for and three goals against. Hell yeah.

16. Como. They got xG'd against Feyenoord on Wednesday -- three goals allowed from 0.5 xG -- but they still play awfully pretty ball. They belong here.

17. Roma. They're still unbeaten in Serie A play, but their defense isn't holding up in this competition.

18. Villarreal. The Yellow Submarine can't get going in league play, but their finishing was on point against Napoli.

19. Inter Milan. Two one-goal losses isn't the end of the world, but I'd recommend beating Shakhtar next week.

20. RB Leipzig. The reverse Dortmund. RBL had lost three of four before the break and have won two by a combined 7-0 since their return.

21. Bodø/Glimt. Cue the "Chelsea Dagger!"

22. Porto. Their league form (eight matches, eight wins) means I'm not worried about their 0-for-2 start here. But upcoming home matches with PSV and Napoli are pretty big.

23. Lens. They've won only two of their past seven matches, and they have to visit Club Brugge next week.

24. Viking. My new lifelong favorite team.

25. PSV Eindhoven. Ivan Perisic played really well against RB Leipzig on Tuesday, but his failed penalty was a two-point miss in a one-goal loss.

26. Feyenoord. The crowd pop after a Feyenoord home goal is something else.

27. Galatasaray. The home crowd showed out against Barcelona as always, but the home team could only hold on for about 50 minutes.

28. Shakhtar Donetsk. Last year's Conference League semifinal run seems to have carried over. They have four points in two matches, and in their first "home" match at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge, they took the fight to AEK Athens awfully well.

29. Fenerbahçe. The 6-0 loss to Villa was exaggerated -- xG: Villa 3.1, Fenerbahce 1.9 -- but ... woof all the same.

30. Lille. Hey, they were tied with Arsenal for 60 minutes, at least.

31. Napoli. They're eighth in Serie A, and they're 33rd in xG differential after two matches here. Max Allegri was an unambitious hire, and the year sure hasn't started like he hoped.

32. AEK Athens. They had a chance to join the six-point club but could only hold onto a lead against Shakhtar for six minutes.

33. Sabah. They understood the assignment: Their home game with Slavia was probably the most winnable match on the docket, and a crowd of 29,670 showed up to Baki Olimpiya Stadionu to help make sure they won it.

34. LASK. Good: They kept fighting against Liverpool and grabbed a couple of late goals. Bad: They were down 6-1 at the time.

35. Slavia Prague. They're 0-for-2, and they still have to play No. 3, 4 and 7 on this list. Yikes.

36. Slovan Bratislava. They play at LASK on Nov. 3 and host Shakhtar on Dec. 9. If they want points in this competition, those are very important matches.

stories.headline: Michael 'Venom' Page: UFC's Dana White 'never really a fan of me'
stories.summary: Michael "Venom" Page has said that his relationship with UFC president Dana White was "nonexistent."
stories.body:
Michael "Venom" Page said that his relationship with UFC president Dana White was "nonexistent" in an exclusive interview with ESPN on Tuesday.

Page joined the UFC in 2023 with his stock at an all-time high after serving as the face of Bellator courtesy of a series of exciting stoppages with his unique freestyle striking style.

But he couldn't replicate that in the UFC with a run of impressive, albeit uninspiring, decision wins in the promotion, along with a solitary defeat to Ian Machado-Garry, leading to the conclusion of his six-fight contract.

White confirmed in September that the UFC would not pursue another deal, and Page announced this week that his next venture is with KSI's Misfits boxing in a "multi-fight, multi-year agreement." And reflecting on his time in the promotion, Page said he felt that White was "never really a fan of me from the beginning."

"Literally nonexistent [relationship with White]," Page told ESPN. "I think we've had a couple of very brief conversations, very, very brief. [Chief business officer Hunter Campbell] was the person that I spoke with quite regularly. I was thankful for him. ... It was him that signed me. It was more Hunter that was the person that was like, 'Look, I want you in the UFC.'

"So I feel like Dana White's never really been a fan of me from the beginning, or I think it came from somebody else. And because I also didn't deliver it in the way he wanted me to deliver, I get he didn't care. You can kind of tell from the announcement, he didn't really make anything of it. He just announced me on the card as if I've always been a fighter there and people were kind of like, 'Wait, what?'

"So I feel like potentially, just based on how he behaves, I'm speculating here, that potentially he wasn't necessarily a fan of mine. And then on top of that, I didn't give him what he wanted as well. So yeah, there was no real relationship with Dana."

UFC didn't respond to ESPN's request for comment.

Page's UFC career wrapped up with a decision win over Nursulton Ruziboev amid boos from a partisan crowd in Paris last month.

Misfits wasn't the only promotion Page spoke to when looking at steps after the UFC with Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions among those interested in the Brit. Page said that a move to MVP, who has recently acquired MMA promotion PFL, was considered, but the timing wasn't right.

"Obviously that [MVP] was probably one of the things at the top of the list. But they just weren't in the right place right now," he said. "It wasn't the right timing more than anything. It wasn't just a financial thing, but it wasn't the right timing for them."

stories.headline: Rafael Câmara to Haas: How F1's next rookie could shake up Ferrari's future
stories.summary: The arrival of Rafa Camara to Haas will give Ferrari an interesting conundrum for the future, writes ESPN's Nate Saunders.
stories.body:
New Haas signing and Ferrari Driver Academy (FDA) star Rafael Câmara will continue his rapid career ascent as a Formula 1 rookie in 2027.

Câmara, 21, will replace Esteban Ocon at Haas next season and partner fellow FDA member Oliver Bearman.

The only way has been up for Câmara recently: he won the Formula 3 championship in 2025 and, as of the announcement of his signing, he leads the Formula 2 championship with two races to run.

The highly-rated Brazilian has been part of the FDA since 2022 -- that year he finished third in Italian F3 and was F1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli's teammate in the 2022 ADAC Championship, also finishing third.

Câmara comes from a racing family. His grandmother, Niége Rossiter, was a successful race driver in the Recife region and won races at a state level.

His elevation continues Brazil's proud F1 heritage -- he will become the nation's 34th driver, joining fellow compatriot Gabriel Bortoleto, who races for Audi.

Bortoleto's debut season had ended seven years without a Brazilian driver -- before Felipe Massa's retirement in 2017, there had been at least one on the grid every year stretching back to 1970.

A Ferrari audition season?

Haas' lineup will be a storyline worth keeping an eye on in 2027.

Putting Bearman and Câmara alongside each other in equal machinery will make a fascinating narrative in terms of who might one day end up racing for the Prancing Horse -- it will give Ferrari the clearest data comparison possible.

Haas has been a Ferrari customer since it made its Formula 1 debut in 2016 but has not had two drivers from the Italian team before.

Rising star Bearman made his debut for Haas in 2024 with two stand-in appearances for Kevin Magnussen before being signed to a full-time drive for 2025.

He has actually raced for Ferrari already, making his F1 debut as Carlos Sainz's stand-in earlier that season at the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix.

He has widely been seen as the next in line for Ferrari for some time, but an opening does not look likely to appear any time soon.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli, it's too late

- F1 to return to Africa in 'early 2030s' as Rwanda race confirmed

- Ferrari protege Câmara completes Haas driver line-up for F1 2027

Charles Leclerc recently signed a bumper extension taking him into the 2030s, while seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton has a contract until the end of 2027 at least -- sources have told ESPN there are options to continue beyond that and the growing feeling is that as things stand Hamilton will race for Ferrari beyond that time.

Bearman recently talked about how Hamilton's 2026 resurgence was good to see, but bad news in terms of his own prospects of moving up.

"As an F1 fan and a Lewis fan as well, it's pretty cool to see him performing at the level he is," Bearman told F1's Beyond the Grid podcast. "Seeing him on the top step in Barcelona was quite a special moment for British F1 in general. It was three Brits on the podium, with the best driver we've ever seen in P1. That's something pretty special.

"Of course, in terms of my future, that's not ideal. But I'm still young. I'm only 21. I'm not in a huge rush, and for me, staying at Haas for the foreseeable is not a bad thing. I feel like there's a lot to learn at this team. There's a lot to still achieve."

Bearman has comprehensively out-performed current teammate Ocon in their year and a half together and most will expect him to do the same against a rookie next year.

Should that not happen, Ferrari's next driver might not be such a safe bet.

stories.headline: 'I'm a competitor': Cody Walker primed and ready for the next step
stories.summary: Cody Walker has lived a year of Carlton's ups and downs before having even been drafted. He's learned a lot about the business of footy and what he needs to do to take the next step, as his own AFL career begins.
stories.body:
Cody Walker had a front row seat to Carlton's tumultuous season. In line meetings, at team dinners, out of the Michael Voss era and into the Josh Fraser fairytale. From door stops to crisis meetings, it was an eye opening introduction to the big business of footy for the son-of-a-gun.

"I actually reflect on it a bit now and consider how low a club can get. Being on the inside with all the outside noise that we had when all the Vossy stuff was going down, it was really quite interesting to see," Walker tells ESPN.

"Then going from that to top of the AFL and beating Brisbane and Fremantle towards the end of the season, seeing how good a club can feel and get. For that to both happen in one season I find it quite interesting. I'm sort of glad it happened in a way that I get to experience both worlds."

In the midst of their early season malaise, Blues players were subjected to abuse walking off the ground after second half fadeouts and even rocked up to Ikon Park with anti-Voss graffiti on the club walls. That included Walker as he trained full-time with the squad.

"All the outside noise tears you apart a little bit. To see fans out the front of Ikon Park sort of giving it to you, and open training to have people yelling out at you and it's your fans, they've got Carlton stuff on, but they're yelling out to you, it's pretty full on."

From 1-8 under Voss, the Blues stormed home under Fraser, winning their next six starts and claiming a remarkable win in a wildcard final against Melbourne.

A fractured playing group was united under a first-time head coach and Walker was along for the ride.

"It was quite an eye opener how sad it can get inside a club. You sort of have to keep to yourself in those moments and just get around the boys," he says.

"We definitely had to stick together as a group, and Fraser's been really good at that. We did a lot together this year, the players grabbed me along to every dinner they had. It was so good, such a good experience."

That finals finish means Carlton receives no discount on matching a bid on the son of high-flyer Andrew, with the pair likely to become the first father-son duo to each be selected in the top five of an AFL Draft.

Walker's talent deserves to see him taken at pick 2, just like his dad.

An electric midfielder blessed with the twitchiness, agility and burst to free himself from stoppages, Walker enjoyed a brilliant campaign with Carlton's VFL side and cemented his status in the 2026 draft.

There's no doubting his mercurial talent and its fit alongside Patrick Cripps, Sam Walsh, and Jagga Smith, but Walker isn't yet the complete package, and he's the first one to acknowledge it.

"I think my burst out of stoppage and ball-winning is my 'one wood'... when I look back on footage and see for myself how dangerous I can look going out of stoppage, it's really eye-opening for me," he tells ESPN.

"My improvements I want going into next year, I want to improve every part of my fundamentals. I've got a little bit of disposal efficiency which can let me down, but I'll put a power of work into kicking and handballing.

"It got to the point where I was doing two or three sessions a week, and that includes Diesel Williams helping me out.

"I've got so many good people around me and I can already feel that I'm getting better at those things. I'm pretty straightforward in what I want to get better at and I like getting harsh feedback from coaches that I can work on.

"No one's really pissing in my pocket about something I need to work on and I don't realise it until I'm maybe on [the MCG] one day and it's a problem for me if I'm missing kicks or missing handballs."

Walker's final game before he turns professional wasn't in Carlton's VFL side, at the national championships with Vic Country or back with the Bendigo Pioneers. It was in the Goulburn Valley Football League playing for hometown Echuca, and he spent most of his lead-up convincing the Blues' General Manager of Football to let him go.

"I actually sat down with Chris Davies about two weeks before the granny. I was like, 'What are the chances I get to play?'" Walker recalls to ESPN.

"He was like, 'Mate, we're not going to stop you. Preferably, I think it's the wrong decision, but it's all your choice.'"

Walker was determined to enjoy one more stint out in the country with his best mates after a massive top-age season, but injured his ankle during training the week after that conversation with Davies. It ruled him out of the qualifying final, but he still had an eye towards their qualification into the big dance.

"I went home for two weeks and I was training with Echuca and I just got addicted. I called up the club and a few people there and I was like 'I think I'm going to play, I'm doing it'. I'm so glad I did it."

Walker had 20 disposals, eight score involvements, and kicked a goal off the wing in Echuca's 13-goal win over the Shepparton Swans.

It underlined the values that have made Walker rise and rise through junior football ranks. His competitive spirit and genuine love of footy through rich bloodlines continually stands out. Carlton supporters have known of Walker's footballing exploits for years, but they may not know what makes him tick.

That attitude was on show in the 2km time trial at the AFL Draft combine. Walker led his group of runners by the length of the straight, finishing nine seconds ahead of second place. It's his inner motivation that drives him to compete against the best, and oftentimes that means competing against himself.

It's why he has a grin on his face when asked why he even ran despite some Blues supporters bemoaning his name rising higher on rival clubs' draft boards.

"It was probably to beat my [personal best]... my PB was 6:13, I was feeling good and I had a bit in the tank," he says.

"Personally I'm a competitor. I do want to see where I'm at as of right now compared to maybe three months later when I do a 2k at the club."

Walker smashed that time, finishing in 6:04 minutes and on the podium despite running in a slower pack.

It's given Carlton more to consider, lacking the points to match a bid at pick 1 but desperate to secure its second elite father-son prospect in as many years after Harry Dean was taken with pick two in 2025.

"I've got plenty of trust in the club with what they can do in my scenario," Walker says.

"I love the Carlton Football Club and I'm really thankful they've given me this year and it would be a really cool thing to end up at my dad's club. There's a lot of history there."

stories.headline: NRL: Spencer Leniu signs with Eels after early Roosters release
stories.summary: Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.
stories.body:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in their 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith from 2021-2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 per year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The westward move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Eels general manager of football Mark O'Neill shared his delight at signing one of the game's "premier enforcers".

"We're thrilled to have Spencer join the Parramatta Eels and become part of what we're building at this club," O'Neill said in a statement.

"He's one of the elite middle forwards in the game and has consistently performed on the biggest stages throughout his career.

The exit of Leniu adds to the exodus of stars from the Roosters premiership lineup.

Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson said Leniu had been a strong contributor during his time at the club.

"Spencer has brought a lot to our group over the last three years, both through the way he plays and the energy and personality he brings every day," Robinson said in a statement on Thursday.

"He brings an intensity and competitiveness to everything he does, and he challenges the people around him to be better.

"To see him finish his time here as a premiership winner is something he should be really proud of, and something we'll always share together."

With his departure announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

""I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," said Leniu.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."
